name: Genesis
v: So Israel set out with everything he owned, and when he reached Beersheba he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.

That night God spoke to Israel in visions: "Jacob. Jacob."

"I'm here," he answered.
"I am God — the God of your father. Don't be afraid to go down to Egypt. I will make you into a great nation there.
I will go down with you, and I will bring you back up again. And Joseph's own hand will close your eyes."
Jacob rose from Beersheba. His sons loaded their father, their children, and their wives onto the wagons Pharaoh had sent to carry him.
They took their livestock and everything they had acquired in Canaan, and Jacob went down to Egypt — he and all his descendants with him —
his sons and grandsons, his daughters and granddaughters. He brought every one of them with him to Egypt.
These are the names of Israel's family who came to Egypt — Jacob and his sons. Reuben, Jacob's firstborn.
Reuben's sons: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
Simeon's sons: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul (whose mother was Canaanite).
Levi's sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
Judah's sons: Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah — though Er and Onan died in Canaan. Perez had sons of his own: Hezron and Hamul.
Issachar's sons: Tola, Puvah, Job, and Shimron.
Zebulun's sons: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These were Leah's sons — born to Jacob in Paddan Aram — along with his daughter Dinah. Thirty-three sons and daughters in all.
Gad's sons: Zephon, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
Asher's sons: Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah — and their sister Serah. Beriah's sons: Heber and Malkiel.
These were Zilpah's children — the maid Laban gave to his daughter Leah — sixteen souls she bore to Jacob.
The sons of Jacob's wife Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
In Egypt, Joseph fathered Manasseh and Ephraim by Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
Benjamin's sons: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
These were Rachel's descendants through Jacob — fourteen in all.
Dan's son: Hushim.
Naphtali's sons: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
These were Bilhah's children — the maid Laban gave to his daughter Rachel — seven souls she bore to Jacob.
Everyone who came with Jacob to Egypt — his direct descendants, not counting the wives of his sons — numbered sixty-six.
Add Joseph's two sons born in Egypt, and the house of Jacob entering Egypt totaled seventy.
Jacob sent Judah ahead to Joseph to get directions to Goshen. When they arrived in the region,
Joseph harnessed his chariot and rode up to meet his father. The moment he saw him, he threw his arms around him and wept on his shoulder a long, long time.
Israel said to Joseph, "Now I can die. I have seen your face. You are alive."
Joseph said to his brothers and his father's household, "I'll go up and tell Pharaoh — I'll say, 'My brothers and my father's household have come to me from Canaan.
They are shepherds. They keep livestock. They've brought their flocks and herds and everything they own.'
When Pharaoh summons you and asks what you do for a living,

tell him: 'Your servants have been keeping livestock since we were boys — just like our fathers before us.' Say this so he will settle you in Goshen — because every shepherd is detestable to the Egyptians."

com.d:
# Genesis 46: Going Down to Rise Up

The spiritual heart of Genesis 46 lies in God's faithful promise-keeping even when His people must walk through seasons of loss and uncertainty. This passage shows us that obedience sometimes means moving in directions that seem contrary to our deepest hopes.

Jacob stands at a crossroads. His beloved son Joseph is alive in Egypt—a revelation that should bring only joy. Yet to see him, Jacob must leave Canaan, the promised land itself, the very territory God had sworn to give his descendants. The old patriarch's heart trembles at what this journey means. So the Lord appears to him at Beersheba with a word both permission and promise: "Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make you into a great nation there. I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back again" (46:3-4).

Notice God does not deny the difficulty of Egypt. He says "go down"—acknowledging it feels like descent. Egypt represents exile, distance from the promised inheritance, a foreign land where God's people will eventually be enslaved. Yet God meets Jacob's fear with covenant assurance: His presence will accompany the patriarch, and His purposes will not be thwarted.

This mirrors our own spiritual journeys. We sometimes find ourselves in unexpected seasons—relocations, job losses, health crises, broken relationships—that feel like walking away from God's best. Our faith questions whether He still holds us, whether His promises remain true when circumstances contradict our hopes. Genesis 46 whispers that God's presence and faithfulness transcend geography. The promised land was never ultimately about location but about relationship with the God who makes the promise.

Jacob responds by getting up and beginning the journey with his entire family—seventy souls in total—trusting that God's "going down" with him guarantees his ultimate rising up.

What circumstance in your life currently feels like going backward? How might God be present in that very place, moving you toward purposes you cannot yet see?
com.s:
Genesis 46 marks a pivotal transition in the patriarchal narratives, documenting Jacob's descent into Egypt with his entire household—a migration that sets the stage for Israel's sojourn and eventual exodus. The chapter divides into three literary units: a theophanic encounter at Beersheba (vv. 1-4), a genealogical register (vv. 5-27), and the reunion with Joseph (vv. 28-34). This structure moves from divine authorization to historical documentation to familial reconciliation, weaving together theological assurance with the concrete realities of migration.

The divine appearance at Beersheba carries profound significance, as this site held deep associations with Abraham and Isaac's encounters with God. The repetition of Jacob's name—"Jacob, Jacob" (v. 2)—echoes the call of Abraham at the Aqedah and Moses at the burning bush, signaling a moment of covenant importance. God's self-identification as *ʾēl ʾĕlōhê ʾābîkā* ("the God of your father") connects this revelation to patriarchal promises while addressing Jacob's evident anxiety about leaving the promised land. The assurance "I myself will bring you up again" (*ʿālōh aʿălekā*) employs the causative verbal form that later becomes technical vocabulary for the exodus, creating intertextual resonance with Israel's redemptive future.

The genealogy enumerating seventy descendants presents interpretive challenges, as the enumeration requires careful calculation to reach the stated total. Scholars debate whether this number functions symbolically, representing completeness (seven times ten) and corresponding to the seventy nations of Genesis 10, thus positioning Israel as a microcosmic counterpart to humanity. The inclusion of Er and Onan, who died in Canaan, alongside those "born to Jacob in Paddan-aram" suggests the list serves theological rather than strictly demographic purposes.

The chapter concludes with Joseph's strategic counsel regarding his family's occupation as shepherds. His advice that they settle in Goshen reflects awareness that shepherds were *tôʿăbâ* ("an abomination") to Egyptians—a detail illuminating both social dynamics and providential geography, as Goshen's marginality would preserve Israel's distinct identity. This careful navigation of Egyptian cultural sensibilities demonstrates Joseph's continued wisdom while positioning Israel for their eventual departure.
com.p:
Genesis 46 unfolds approximately 1876 years before Christ, during the patriarchal age when God's covenant promises to Abraham remained largely embryonic—a family of seventy souls rather than a nation of millions. This chapter marks a pivotal transition in redemptive history: the descent of Jacob's household into Egypt, which would set the stage for the Exodus four centuries later. We stand here at the hinge between the patriarchal narratives and Israel's formation as a covenant nation through bondage and deliverance.

As Jacob prepares to leave Canaan for Egypt, God meets him at Beersheba with a nighttime vision, speaking words of profound covenantal reassurance: "I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make you into a great nation there." The Almighty who called Abraham out of Ur now calls Abraham's grandson into Egypt—not as abandonment of the promised land, but as the mysterious pathway toward its ultimate possession. Here we glimpse the divine pattern that courses through all of Scripture: God accomplishes His purposes through apparent reversals, through descent before ascent, through death before resurrection.

The genealogical registry of seventy souls who entered Egypt carries typological weight that reverberates across the canon. This number reappears when Moses appoints seventy elders to share his burden, when Jesus sends seventy disciples to proclaim the kingdom, and in the traditional count of the nations in Genesis 10. Jacob's household represents a microcosm of humanity—a family through whom all families of the earth would receive blessing. Their journey into Egypt typologically foreshadows the holy family's flight to the same land, when another Joseph would protect another threatened Child through whom salvation would come.

Joseph's chariot meeting Jacob at Goshen prefigures the greater reunion awaiting God's people. The one who was sold, rejected, and given up for dead now appears in glory to receive his father with weeping and embrace. Christ, rejected by His brethren according to the flesh, will one day reveal Himself to Israel with tears of reconciliation, and "all Israel shall be saved."

The church today lives as sojourners in a foreign land, awaiting our own exodus. Like Jacob's family preserved in Egypt, we are sustained in the world but not consumed by it, growing into the fullness of our inheritance until the day when the true Joseph gathers His people into the eternal Promised Land.
